content: Cephalexin is a cephalosporin antibiotic that is prescribed to treat specific bacterial infections, including pneumonia, as well as infections of the bones, ears, skin, and urinary tract. It is important to note that antibiotics like cephalexin are ineffective against colds, the flu, or other viral infections. In some cases, cephalexin may be prescribed for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Cephalexin is available in capsule, tablet, and liquid forms, and it is taken orally. The usual dosing schedule is either every 6 hours (four times a day) or every 12 hours (twice a day) for a duration of 7 to 10 days. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take cephalexin exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it, or take it more frequently than prescribed. If you are using the liquid form, shake the bottle well before each use to ensure the medication is evenly mixed. Swallow the capsules and tablets whole with a full glass of water. Continue taking cephalexin even if you feel better, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Before starting cephalexin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to cephalexin, other cephalosporin antibiotics (e.g., cefadroxil or cephradine), penicillin, or any other drugs. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially other antibiotics, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), probenecid, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, colitis, or stomach problems. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking cephalexin, contact your doctor immediately. Additionally, if you are scheduled for surgery, including dental procedures, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking cephalexin. Cephalexin may cause stomach upset. To minimize this, take the medication with food or milk. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Cephalexin may cause side effects. Minor side effects include upset stomach, diarrhea, vomiting, and mild skin rash. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention and include severe skin rash, itching, hives, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, unusual bleeding or bruising, sore throat, painful mouth or throat sores, and vaginal infections. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store cephalexin in the container it came in, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Capsules and tablets should be stored at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Liquid medication should be refrigerated, tightly closed, and discarded after 14 days. Do not freeze the liquid form. Dispose of unused or expired medication properly; consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911 immediately. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor may order lab tests to monitor your response to cephalexin. If you have diabetes, use Clinistix or TesTape (not Clinitest) to test your urine for sugar while taking this medication. Do not share your medication with others. Your prescription is likely not refillable. If your symptoms persist after completing the course of cephalexin, contact your doctor.
